newsitem.title: MEXICO: Main points of Mexican 1997 budget speech.
newsitem.headline: Main points of Mexican 1997 budget speech.

text.p: Following are the main points of Finance Minister Guillermo Ortiz's budget speech to Congress, as detailed in texts from the Finance Ministry:

-- Economic growth of at least four percent seen in 1997, as against about 3.7 percent this year. Ortiz said that was "an achievable target," as outlook was favorable for investment and other components of aggregate demand.
-- Inflation in 1997 estimated at 15 percent compared with 26.2 percent in 1996.
-- Average exchange rate forecast for public finance projections of 8.53 pesos per dollar in 1997.
-- Peso to continue in free floating exchange rate. Ortiz said that was the best option for an open economy and necessary for the export sector to keep its competitive edge.

-- Budget deficit of 0.5 percent of gross domestic product expected, compared with a deficit of 0.06 percent this year. That was expected mainly because of the cost of pension reforms and the bank bailout program.
"Notwithstanding these costs, by making more efficient use of funds, and under the current tax regime, investment and public savings will increase significantly," Ortiz said.
-- Estimated current account deficit of 1.18 percent of GDP in 1997, against 0.31 percent this year.
-- Total public investment at 3.7 percent of GDP in 1997, compared with 3.61 percent in 1996, mostly on infrastructure projects in the oil, electricity, highway, water and housing sectors.
-- Ortiz said a "gradual recovery" in real wages next year would allow "a moderate" recovery of consumption.
-- 1997 total net spending - total public sector spending less debt amortizations - 725.79 billion pesos, up 5.2 percent from 1996.
-- Total planned social spending to increase 9.3 percent from 1996 to 227.42 billion pesos, and to equal 55.8 percent of total planned spending.
